caption:
Google released Gemini 4 Neon on November 18, its fourth new Gemini 4 model in about a month.
It sits between Hydrogen and Carbon, costs $3 per million input tokens and is in the Gemini app for AI Pro and Ultra users.
Google says it cuts the cost per task by 32% compared with Carbon.

site_article.answer_summary: Gemini 4 Neon is a Google model released on November 18, 2026 that sits between Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon. paragraphs.text: Google released Gemini 4 Neon on November 18, 2026, describing it as a model that brings frontier level intelligence to complex software engineering, knowledge work and science, with fast completion of tasks from start to finish. The announcement was written by Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president at Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google.

Neon is the fourth new Gemini 4 model in about a month, following Argon, Carbon and Hydrogen, according to The Decoder. 9to5Google noted that it followed Carbon on November 10 and Hydrogen on November 12.

Google positions Neon for complex coding, analytical reasoning and production enterprise workflows. 9to5Google reported that Google describes its performance as comparable to Carbon across coding, reasoning and agentic tasks, but at Flash speeds and a lower cost.

In the Gemini app, Neon is available to AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers and replaces Argon. According to 9to5Google, the model picker now offers Auto, Everyday help running Hydrogen, Deeper analysis running Neon, and Code and complex work running Carbon. The same report said Gemini 3.1 Pro is leaving the app.

Developers can use Neon through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, and it is also offered in Google Antigravity for paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, in Android Studio and in Gemini for business, Google said. A version for cybersecurity work is rolling out to trusted defenders in Google's Fairwind Program.

Neon costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.15 per million tokens, and has a context window of 1 million tokens, according to Google. The Decoder reported that inputs can include text, images, video, audio and PDFs, while image and audio generation are not supported.

The pricing comparison inside the family is shifting. Carbon and Argon carry an introductory rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens that rises to $4 and $20 on December 1, while Hydrogen costs $1.50 and $7.50, The Decoder reported. 9to5Google said that once the promotion ends, Neon will be 25% cheaper than Carbon.

Google said that at the default high thinking level, Neon's cost per task is 32% lower than Carbon's. The company reported a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its highest setting, third overall, and first place on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with 58.6.

Other results Google listed include second place on the Vals Index at 70.9%, 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1, 84.0% on RiemannBench for science and math, and first place on Zapier's AutomationBench at 56.3%. These are figures published by Google, and The Decoder noted that further benchmark results were still expected after launch.

Neon is less about a new top score than about filling a gap in a crowded lineup. Google now offers four Gemini 4 models with overlapping uses, and Neon's pitch rests on finishing work in fewer steps, which matters more to companies paying per task than to people chatting in the app. The rapid release pace also makes the naming harder for ordinary users to follow, which may explain why the app labels its choices by job rather than by model name.
The test comes on December 1, when Carbon's introductory price ends and developers can compare what Neon and Carbon really cost on the same workloads.
